intro:
The developer-tools category is the largest on AgentStack because it's the foundation of any AI coding agent workflow. Git, GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, code review, CI/CD, infrastructure-as-code — these are the tools that turn a chat interface into something that can actually ship code to production.

The split we see most often is "how do I let my agent commit, branch, and open PRs" (GitHub MCP, GitLab MCP, Git MCP, Bitbucket MCP) versus "how do I let my agent review and judge code" (GitHub, GitLab, Greptile, Koduste). The first group is about giving the agent write access to your repos. The second group is about letting the agent act as a code reviewer.

What separates the projects we list from the ones we don't: we only include tools that have production-grade authentication (personal access tokens with scoped permissions, GitHub App installations with fine-grained perms), official or widely-adopted SDK patterns, and active maintenance (a commit in the last 90 days). We've excluded community forks of the official servers that haven't been updated in 12+ months and proprietary vendor SDKs disguised as MCP servers.
selectionNotes: We score developer tools on: authentication model (PAT, GitHub App, OAuth), scope of API access (read-only vs read-write vs fine-grained), how it handles rate limits, whether it supports self-hosted GitHub Enterprise / GitLab self-managed, and the maintainer's track record of following GitHub/MCP spec changes.

intro:
The databases category is split three ways: SQL (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, Supabase, Neon, CockroachDB, ClickHouse), NoSQL/document (MongoDB, Firebase-style Firestore, CouchDB, ArangoDB), and vector (Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, Weaviate). Each MCP server in this category is a thin bridge from your agent to the database — it doesn't store data itself, it just gives the agent the ability to query and (with permission) modify the database you already run.

The honest answer for most teams: if you're on Postgres (which most modern stacks are), install the Postgres MCP server for raw queries, or the Supabase MCP server if you want auth/RLS/storage too. If you have multi-database infrastructure, pick per-engine servers — there's no point in a single "database MCP" that abstracts away the differences.

What separates the projects we list from the ones we don't: we require a documented auth model (connection string via env var, or short-lived OAuth where supported), row-level safety (the server warns before running DROP / TRUNCATE), and active maintenance. We've excluded DIY servers with hardcoded credentials in README examples and projects that try to bundle every database engine into one server.
selectionNotes: We score database tools on: auth model (env var vs OAuth vs SSH tunnel), query safety (does it block destructive statements, require confirmation, or audit log?), connection pooling behaviour, support for read replicas, and the documentation around row-level access (RLS / Postgres grants vs app-level checks).

intro:
Web scraping and search are the categories where the difference between "works on the README's example" and "works in production" is biggest. Most agents need to fetch the live web for one of three reasons: research (read articles, papers, docs), data extraction (product prices, job listings, news), or grounding (give the LLM a fresh URL to answer questions about).

The split is between search APIs (Brave Search, Tavily, Exa, Kagi, SerpAPI, Perplexity), scraping frameworks (Firecrawl, Apify, Browserless, Oxylabs, ScrapeGraphAI, Diffbot), and lightweight fetcher MCPs (Fetch, Puppeteer, Jina). Search APIs return clean, ranked results in JSON. Scraping frameworks handle anti-bot, JS rendering, and structured extraction. Fetchers just give the agent raw HTML to parse.

For most agents picking up web capability for the first time: start with one search API (Brave or Tavily are the easiest) and one fetcher (Fetch MCP is the minimal MCP-native option; Puppeteer if you need to handle JavaScript). Add a scraping framework later if research results need structured extraction.

What separates the projects we list from the ones we don't: respect for robots.txt, sane rate limits documented up-front (no auto-crawling that gets you IP-banned in an hour), pricing that's actually usable (the agent isn't going to burn through $200 of Proxies.ai tokens because it followed three redirects), and a maintained release cadence.
selectionNotes: We score web / search tools on: robots.txt compliance, rate-limit behaviour (with and without a key), the JSON output shape (clean vs raw HTML), pricing transparency (per-request vs per-1k-tokens vs per-month), and whether the scraped content is cached or always fresh.

intro:
The productivity category is where the 'agent + SaaS' idea gets tested hardest, because it requires the agent to have correct, structured access to where your team actually works: Notion, Linear, Jira, Asana, Todoist, Airtable, Obsidian, Google Sheets, calendars. The MCP servers in this category are essentially "the API documentation, as a tool your agent can call".

The split is between work-tracking tools (Linear, Jira, Asana, Todoist, ClickUp), knowledge / docs (Notion, Obsidian, Anki), and structured data (Airtable, Google Sheets, HubSpot). The first group is what engineering and product teams already use — the agent plugs in to read tickets, write comments, update status. The second group is for personal or team knowledge bases — the agent reads your notes, summarizes meetings, drafts docs. The third is for when your real data lives in a spreadsheet-style interface.

The honest answer for most teams: if you're on Linear, install the Linear MCP. If you're on Notion + Jira, install both — they don't replace each other. If you're on a stack that doesn't have an official MCP (Asana, ClickUp, Monday), check the publisher's API support first; many of these have community servers that lag behind the official API by weeks.

What separates the projects we list: official partner programs where the publisher maintains the server themselves, OAuth flow that respects your existing app permissions, and search support (an MCP server that can read but not search a wiki isn't useful to an agent).
selectionNotes: We score productivity tools on: auth flow (OAuth vs API key vs personal token), the API surface covered (read/write/comment/assign), search quality (does the MCP expose the same search your SaaS UI uses?), webhook support, and whether write operations are explicit (no silent state changes).

intro:
Communication tools are how the agent tells humans what's going on — Slack messages, Discord posts, Telegram notifications, email drafts, SMS alerts. The split is between chat platforms (Slack, Discord, Telegram), email (Gmail, Mailchimp), video/voice (Twilio, Zoom), and SMS/notification gateways (Twilio, MessageBird, Vonage).

The line we draw: this category is for tools that *deliver* messages to humans, not tools that read or analyze them. If you want an agent that can summarize a Slack channel's last 24 hours, that's probably a combination of Slack MCP + an LLM context window — not a separate "communication analytics" MCP. What we list here are the write-side pipes.

The honest answer for most teams setting up agent notifications: install Slack MCP for engineering alerts, plus one of email/SMS for customer-facing messages. Twilio is the most flexible for SMS; Gmail is the most flexible for email. WhatsApp/Meta gateways have stricter compliance (10DLC registration in the US) and aren't usually worth the work for an internal team.

What separates the projects we list: explicit permission scopes (the agent can post to one channel but not read your DMs by default), dry-run modes for testing, rate-limit awareness (so the agent doesn't flood a channel), and clear separation between test/sandbox and production credentials.
selectionNotes: We score communication tools on: permission scope granularity (per-channel, per-user, per-action vs all-or-nothing), rate-limit handling (does the server queue, batch, or just throw?), the test vs production separation, whether threads and replies are first-class, and the webhook inbound side (in addition to the agent writing out).

intro:
The AI & Reasoning category is the strangest in AgentStack because it includes tools that help your agent think — embedding providers (OpenAI, Cohere, Voyage, Mistral), vector databases (Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, Weaviate), LLM observability (Langfuse, Helicone), chain-of-thought helpers (Sequential Thinking, Anthropic MCP), and direct LLM access from inside the agent for sub-task delegation.

The split is between storage (vector DBs and embedding caches), evaluation / observability (Langfuse, Helicone), and on-the-fly reasoning helpers (Sequential Thinking, LangChain). Vector DBs are where the agent's long-term memory lives. Observability tools are where you see the agent's reasoning trace when it goes wrong. Sequential-thinking style helpers are the few tools in this category that change the agent's process itself rather than its inputs/outputs.

The honest answer for most teams: if your agent does RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), you need one vector DB (Pinecone or Qdrant are the most popular; Chroma for local dev). If you ship agent features to real users, you need Langfuse — full stop, the alternative is debugging from production logs which costs you weeks. If your agent does multi-step tasks, install Sequential Thinking before you ship to customers.

What separates the projects we list: SDKs that match the framework you already use (Python-first vs TS-first), support for the embedding provider you already pay for, latency that won't block the agent's main flow, and clear separation between dev/prod environments.
selectionNotes: We score AI tools on: framework support (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, raw SDK), embedding provider integration, the metadata schema (what tags you can filter on), observability coverage (input, output, traces, spans), and the cost model for production.

intro:
Cloud & Infrastructure is where the agent stops being a chat interface and starts being an operator — it can spin up AWS resources, deploy to Vercel, manage Cloudflare zones, talk to a Kubernetes cluster, push to Fly.io, or run Terraform. The MCP servers in this category are essentially the cloud provider's CLI wrapped as a tool your agent can call.

The split is between hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure), platform-as-a-service providers (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, Fly, Render, Railway, DigitalOcean), container orchestration (Kubernetes, Docker), and infrastructure-as-code (Terraform). The hyperscalers expose the most surface area but the most operational complexity. PaaS providers give the agent smaller, cleaner surfaces ('deploy to production' is one tool call). IaC tooling lets the agent change the actual definitions rather than the resources.

The honest answer for most teams: if you're on Vercel, install the Vercel MCP — it's the cleanest experience in this category. If you're multi-cloud, you probably want one MCP per provider rather than a 'super-CLI' that abstracts them. If your stack runs on K8s, the Kubernetes MCP will pay for itself in kubectl context switching alone.

What separates the projects we list: read-only-by-default mode (an agent that has permission to delete RDS instances with no confirmation is a liability), credential handling that prefers short-lived tokens (OIDC, AWS SSO) over long-lived access keys, and a maintained release cadence that tracks the provider's own API changes.
selectionNotes: We score cloud-infra tools on: read-only default behaviour, credential model (long-lived keys vs short-lived OIDC vs SSO), the CLI-to-MCP tooling quality (does it lag the native CLI?), cost-control hooks (budgets, tags), and audit logging of every action the agent takes.

intro:
Monitoring is one of the most underrated categories on this site. Once your agent is in production, you need to know what it's doing — what tools it's calling, how long they take, how often they fail, and when something starts misbehaving. The MCP servers here give your agent the same monitoring surface your SRE team already uses.

The split is between logs (Datadog, Betterstack, Logflare, Instana), metrics (Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana, Axiom), error tracking (Sentry), uptime (Betterstack, Datadog), and APM (Datadog, Honeycomb, Instana, Sentry). Most real stacks combine two or three of these — Datadog covers logs + metrics + APM, but it's expensive. Grafana + Loki + Prometheus + Sentry is the common open-source combo.

The honest answer for most teams: if you're on the Datadog subscription already, install Datadog MCP — it gives the agent both write and read access to your existing dashboards. If you're building observability greenfield, install Sentry MCP (for errors) + Honeycomb MCP (for traces) — they're the two with the cleanest schemas for agent queries.

What separates the projects we list: support for the agent identifying itself in audit logs (so you know what the agent did vs a human), filtering by service/environment/host (the agent doesn't get a firehose of every log line), alert-route awareness (the agent can suppress alerts, not just read them), and rate limits that don't break down under agent-scale load.
selectionNotes: We score monitoring tools on: query language support (PromQL, LogQL, SPL, vendor-specific), the metadata dimensions you can filter on (host, env, service, version), agent identity in audit logs, alert-state read/write separation, and rate-limit behaviour at query time vs ingest time.

intro:
Payments is the category with the highest stakes per tool call — a single bad tool call here can move real money. The MCP servers give an agent controlled access to your payment provider's API: read customer data, list subscriptions, create payment links, issue refunds (with restrictions), look up invoices, manage products.

The split is between full-stack payment processors (Stripe, Adyen, Braintree, Square, Paddle, Lemon Squeezy) and subscription/billing platforms (Lemonsqueezy, Paddle, Chargebee). Stripe dominates in this category — both because it has the best MCP server and because it's the default for most new SaaS. Adyen is the enterprise alternative. Paddle and Lemon Squeezy are the merchant-of-record options for software sellers.

The honest answer for most teams: if you're on Stripe (which is most SaaS teams), install Stripe MCP with a restricted API key. The default read-only mode is enough for 80% of agent use cases — looking up a subscription, refunding a charge, sending an invoice. The remaining 20% (creating new charges from chat) should require a separate, narrowly-permissioned key.

What separates the projects we list: read-only-by-default, restricted-API-key support (not just full-secret keys), permission scopes that follow Stripe's own key model (so you can give the agent refund-yes-but-charge-no), a sandbox/test mode that doesn't affect production, and audit logging.
selectionNotes: We score payment tools on: sandbox vs production isolation, restricted key support (per-action vs full), scope of allowed operations (read vs write vs refund vs create-charge), PCI scope implications (does the MCP see card numbers, or only tokens?), and audit-log quality.
